doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Composing from a germ
summary: Longo starts pieces from a germ coming from a special place, a lesson from Hall Overton, and composing equals arranging.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Great words of wisdom, Mike, I appreciate it. Just to wrap up I wonder about your composing process. If I got a little grant and I could commission you to write something brand new, do you have a place where you would start? How do I start something brand new?
I do that all the time.
Well is there anything that gets you going?
And where does it come from?
From that place I just told you.

I usually tell people I don’t write anything unless it comes from that. Where I learned that, when I was studying with Hall Overton, because I would be taking lessons when we’d come into town. And so we were in Holland and it was the summertime and they had Dizzy’s whole quintet was in this big dormitory and we were the only ones there. And I found a dance studio on the top floor with a piano in it, and all night long I could go up there and write. So at the time I was writing an atonal canon. And so when I came back to New York I had a lesson and I said I wasn’t finished, let me just improvise this, and I wrote down — so Hall looked at it and he says, “Man, you were writing a great piece and you got off the thread at the end.”

Yeah. He said, “It’s like you said a very profound thing and then tell a dumb joke at the end.” And I said, “Ohhh. When it’s coming from this part of my brain, that’s the truth. When it’s coming from that, that was my ego trying to finish it.” And so I told the guys, “I don’t write anything unless it’s coming from that place.” That’s when I became in touch with that place. I said, “The only thing that can change my mind is if somebody says three grand.” That’s when the pencil starts writing by itself.

But I’ve had some professional gigs like Bob Cranshaw once, he did a Latin Christmas record. So he calls me on a Friday night and the record date is Sunday. And Ben Brown, the bass player, he’s on the first floor, I gave him the gig as the copyist. So he’d be coming up on the elevator and taking the next page of the score that I’d be writing. But we did get the gig done. But again, I started with a germ. Basically my approach is composition and arranging are the same thing. Composition is basically arranging with your own themes, and arranging is basically composition with somebody else’s themes. So the first thing I look for is a germ. And once I’ve got that a piece of music is in progress on the paper and I just let it uncover itself.
You don’t need the piano to get the germ?
